clue.text: Desert traveller turns to a royal city

parts.note: the camel is the classic beast of burden that crosses deserts

indicators.note: the word to is turned round, so its two letters are read the other way

explanation.surface: A camel driver steers his mount towards a city of kings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' makes OT from 'to'. CAMELOT is the legendary court of King Arthur.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend this was the seat of King Arthur's court, hence a royal city.

clue.text: It clears the bottleneck

parts.note: sounds like something easing a traffic jam, but means the tool that pulls the stopper out of a bottle's neck

explanation.surface: Something that ends a traffic jam.
explanation.walkthrough: A bottleneck is a narrow road, but here it is literally a bottle's neck, cleared by drawing the cork.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiral tool for drawing stoppers from wine bottles clears the neck of the bottle.

clue.text: Old mice can be very tuneful !

indicators.note: says the letters of old mice can be made into something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Elderly rodents turn out to sing beautifully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can be' signals rearranging OLD MICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of pleasing melody, hence musically pleasant to hear.

clue.text: Proverbially they're in no position for ego-boosting

definitions.text: Proverbially they're in no position for ego-boosting

parts.words: Proverbially they're in no position for ego-boosting
parts.note: refers to the proverb that eavesdroppers never hear good of themselves

explanation.surface: Some people are poorly placed to have their egos flattered.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'listeners never hear good of themselves' says eavesdroppers only hear criticism, so they get no boost to their egos.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who overhear, eavesdroppers, never hear praise of themselves according to the proverb.

clue.text: Master of Arts ?

indicators.note: the master is made of the letters of arts, rearranged, and the question mark flags the trick

explanation.surface: Someone holding a university master's degree.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is the degree MA, but 'Master' is the definition and 'of' says it is made from ARTS rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian emperor was absolute ruler, a master of his realm.

clue.text: Keeping one's wool on — or not ?

definitions.text: Keeping one's wool on — or not

parts.words: Keeping one's wool on — or not
parts.note: one sense describes a sheep still wearing its coat; the other describes being shorn of it, or figuratively swindled of money

explanation.surface: A question about whether a sheep keeps its coat.
explanation.walkthrough: The word works both ways: something that has a fleece is fleeced, and a sheep sheared of its fleece is fleeced too, as is a person cheated of cash.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both covered with wool and stripped of it, or robbed by trickery.

clue.text: Genealogy adopted by Max's half-brother

parts.note: a record of descent that would show half-siblings and adopted children alike

explanation.surface: A half-brother takes up researching his ancestry.
explanation.walkthrough: A chart of relationships is where an adopted child or a half-brother finds his place.
explanation.definitionFit: A chart showing a family's descent and relationships is a genealogy.

clue.text: It's of consuming interest to a pangolin

definitions.text: It's of consuming interest to a pangolin

parts.words: It's of consuming interest to a pangolin
parts.note: the pangolin eats insects, so its consuming interest is the creature it consumes

explanation.surface: Something a scaly anteater is very keen on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consuming interest' usually means a passion; here it means food. Emmet is an old dialect word for an ant, which pangolins eat.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for an ant, the insect that the scaly anteater feeds on.

clue.text: Expensive road-guide ?

parts.note: a reflector stud marking the middle of a road shares its name with a costly gemstone

explanation.surface: A pricey road atlas.
explanation.walkthrough: Cat's-eyes are the reflective studs that guide drivers at night on British roads; a cat's-eye is also a precious gemstone.
explanation.definitionFit: The reflecting road stud guides drivers, and the chatoyant gem of the same name is costly.

clue.text: Crown of the hat

parts.note: a bowler hat, and also the race that crowns the flat-racing season in England

explanation.surface: The top part of a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A derby is the American name for a bowler hat; the Derby at Epsom is the crowning race of England's flat season.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowler hat is called by this name in America, and the Epsom race is the crown of English horse racing.

clue.text: Moon rivers ?

parts.note: small streams, and also the narrow channels astronomers see on the lunar surface

explanation.surface: Echoes the song title Moon River.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the song, but the clue wants small streams, a word also used (often spelt rilles) for the long channels on the Moon's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Rills are little brooks, and lunar rilles are channel-like valleys on the Moon that look like dry riverbeds.

clue.text: Mother follows the battle closely in an academic sense

definitions.text: Mother follows the battle closely in an academic sense

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other in the answer, so mother is written after the battle

parts.note: the Alma was a Crimean War battle of 1854, fought at the river of that name
mater is the Latin word for mother, also used in old British slang

explanation.surface: A mother keeps close track of a war's progress, with a scholarly slant.
explanation.walkthrough: The Alma is a river in the Crimea where an 1854 battle was fought. 'closely' says nothing comes between the pieces; the whole clue describes the phrase's meaning of a nurturing mother in academic usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A former school or university is called one's nurturing mother in academic usage, from the Latin for kindly mother.

clue.text: His sister was " the subject of all verse '

definitions.text: His sister was " the subject of all verse '

parts.words: His sister was " the subject of all verse '
parts.note: quotes William Browne's epitaph on Mary, Countess of Pembroke, which begins by calling her the subject of all verse and names her brother

explanation.surface: A man whose sister inspired every poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The epitaph on the Countess of Pembroke opens 'Underneath this sable hearse / Lies the subject of all verse: / Sidney's sister, Pembroke's mother'. Her brother was the Elizabethan poet Sir Philip Sidney.
explanation.definitionFit: The Elizabethan poet Sir Philip shared this surname with his sister Mary, the countess praised in the famous epitaph.

clue.text: Charm practised by the skilful apartment-hunter ?

definitions.text: Charm practised by the skilful apartment-hunter

parts.words: Charm practised by the skilful apartment-hunter
parts.note: reads the answer as the craft of someone who hunts for a flat, a 'flatter', while really meaning insincere praise

explanation.surface: A tip for winning over landlords when looking for a home.
explanation.walkthrough: A flat is a British apartment, so a flat-hunter could be a 'flatter', and his skill would be 'flatter-y'; the everyday sense is the smooth-talking charm used to win people over.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive praise used to win favour is a form of charm.

clue.text: Little 11 turns up with room for discipline, and needing it

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up reads the letters from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: 11 across is SIDNEY, and its shortened, little form is Sid
the orderly room is where military discipline is administered

explanation.surface: A small person shows up with space for training and needs it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns up' reverses SID (short for SIDNEY, the answer at 11) to DIS. The orderly room is the army office dealing with discipline, giving ORDERLY; 'needing it' means needing discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: Unruly behaviour calls for discipline, so being in want of it means being unruly.

clue.text: Decoration for distinguished companion in a pitiful state

indicators.note: the companion is placed within the pitiful state, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: rue is sorrow or regret, the state of feeling pity
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order of distinction

explanation.surface: A decorated companion of the realm has fallen on hard times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Decoration' suggests a medal, and the companion seems to have one; but CH (Companion of Honour) is a British honour supplying letters, and the decoration is a dressmaker's frill.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruche is a gathered frill of fabric used as trimming on a garment, so a decoration.

clue.text: Finding's keeping in the interest of the self-centred

definitions.text: Finding's keeping in the interest of the self-centred

parts.words: Finding's keeping in the interest of the self-centred
parts.note: describes a person who finds it best to keep in, turned inward rather than outward, for whom the self is the main interest

explanation.surface: A judgment about what serves self-absorbed people.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paints someone who keeps themselves to themselves and whose interest is turned inward.
explanation.definitionFit: Such a person turns their attention inward, keeping to themselves rather than seeking company.

clue.text: In which the room at the top is limited

definitions.text: In which the room at the top is limited

parts.words: In which the room at the top is limited
parts.note: describes a system of rule where only a few people hold power

explanation.surface: A building whose top floor is cramped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Room at the top' is a phrase for a place among the powerful; where only a few hold power, that room is limited.
explanation.definitionFit: Government by a small group of powerful people leaves few places at the top.

clue.text: Company car ?

parts.note: plays on the saying that two is company, so a car for company holds two

explanation.surface: A vehicle provided by an employer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company car' suggests an employee perk, but the saying 'two's company' makes a car for company one that seats two.
explanation.definitionFit: A car with seats for only a pair of people suits the saying that two is company.

clue.text: Where to get the edge in N.20?

definitions.text: Where to get the edge in N.20

parts.words: Where to get the edge in N.20
parts.note: names the place where a blade is sharpened, and also a district of north London with the postcode N20

explanation.surface: Asks where to find an advantage in a London postal district.
explanation.walkthrough: N20 is a north London postcode covering the suburb of Whetstone; a whetstone is also the stone a blade is sharpened on, giving it an edge.
explanation.definitionFit: A sharpening stone puts the edge on knives, and it is also the name of a north London suburb in postcode N20.

clue.text: Shoulder-strap

parts.note: a plain description of the ornamental strap worn on the shoulder of a uniform

explanation.definitionFit: An ornamental strap or pad on the shoulder of a uniform jacket.

clue.text: The White House

parts.note: not the US president's residence but a home built of white snow blocks

explanation.surface: The residence of the US president.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals point to Washington, but a snow house is white all over.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit dome-shaped dwelling built from blocks of snow is literally a white house.

clue.text: Little Green Book ?

parts.note: echoes Mao's Little Red Book, but means a small leaf, or a printed pamphlet

explanation.surface: A small book with a green cover.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls Mao's Little Red Book. A small green thing is a little leaf, and a leaflet is also a small printed booklet.
explanation.definitionFit: A pamphlet is a small booklet, and a young leaf on a plant is little and green.

clue.text: A cuppa for the boy of course in the box

parts.note: a cuppa is British slang for a cup of tea
a caddie is the lad who carries clubs on a golf course

explanation.surface: Someone takes a cup of tea out to a boy at school, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but means 'on the golf course': the boy there is a CADDY (golf bag carrier). A cuppa is British slang for tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A small container for keeping tea leaves is a kind of box.

clue.text: He was booked to get a portion

parts.note: a bit is a small portion of something

explanation.surface: A man arrested and charged hoped to get his share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'booked' suggests an arrest, but means he has a book of the Bible named after him: the Book of Tobit, in the Apocrypha.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocryphal Book of Tobit is named after its hero, so he has a book.

clue.text: Movement to rent a cave?

indicators.note: movement of the letters of rent a shifts them into a new order

explanation.surface: Moving house to rent a cave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement to' rearranges RENT A. Antre is a literary word for a cave, used by Shakespeare in Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic word for a cavern, as in Othello's 'antres vast'.

clue.text: A bottle for the artist in the restaurant

indicators.note: the artist is placed inside the restaurant, one piece within the other

parts.note: a cafe is a small restaurant
RA, Royal Academician, is a standard abbreviation for an artist

explanation.surface: Ordering a bottle for a painter dining out.
explanation.walkthrough: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts, which is why it is a stock abbreviation for an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A glass flask for serving wine or water at table is a type of bottle.

clue.text: did I live and gladly die (Stevenson)

annotationWithheld.why: "— did I live and gladly die" (Stevenson): a quotation gap-fill with no wordplay; the next word 'gladly' contains the missing word, so the cryptic-definition form is refused and there is no hidden-word indicator to parse it otherwise
annotationWithheld.clue: did I live and gladly die (Stevenson)

clue.text: Taking in a couple of parties

definitions.text: Taking in a couple of parties

parts.words: Taking in a couple of parties
parts.note: reads like going to two social gatherings, but means involving two sides to an agreement

explanation.surface: Someone attends two parties in one evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parties' suggests celebrations, but in law and politics a party is a side in an agreement; a deal involving two sides is two-sided.
explanation.definitionFit: Two-sided, as in an agreement between two nations or groups, is the meaning.

clue.text: Pauline Court

parts.note: a Pauline is a pupil of St Paul's School, London, whose junior school was named after its founder

explanation.surface: A woman named Pauline Court.
explanation.walkthrough: John Colet founded St Paul's School in London (its pupils are Paulines), and its prep school was called Colet Court.
explanation.definitionFit: The founder of St Paul's School gave his surname to its preparatory school, so the court of the Paulines bears it.

clue.text: Shaky tourist heading to St. Maryville

indicators.note: the head of the word tourist is its first letter, taken alone

parts.note: Ottery St Mary is a town in Devon, so the town that goes with St Mary is Ottery

explanation.surface: A wobbly sightseer makes for a town named after the Virgin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading' takes T from 'tourist'. OTTERY ST MARY is a small town in Devon, England, birthplace of Coleridge; 'St. Maryville' asks for the town part of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsteady on one's feet, inclined to wobble, means shaky.

clue.text: "So sinks the-in the ocean bed'"(Milton)

parts.note: a line from Milton's elegy Lycidas with a word missing, to be filled with the poet's name for the sun

explanation.surface: A gap-fill from Milton's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lycidas Milton writes 'So sinks the day-star in the ocean bed', meaning the sun setting into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A poetic term for the sun, or the morning star, used by Milton in Lycidas.
